title: Half-Baked Theory Roundup — compact reading notes
content:
Quick header: brain-dump after a long afternoon of skimming papers + 1h sync with Marco. Goal: capture the half-formed theories I keep tossing around so they don't evaporate. Use this as a sprint kickoff note if anything is plausible.

Why I care (one-liner): small improvements in context maintenance + eviction heuristics could reduce token spend by 10–30% for certain long-dialog products if we can keep high-utility KV entries and compress/remove the rest cheaply.

Short summaries (very terse):
- Learned anchor compression (paper link above): idea is to train a tiny predictor that maps recent token windows -> fixed-size anchor vectors that approximate the long tail of KV context for retrieval. Pros: amortized compactness, works well when topic drift is smooth. Cons: model needs training per customer domain or heavy finetune. My thought: try a two-stage approach where we use anchors for low-value chat sessions and exact KV for flagged high-value sessions.

- Soft eviction by importance (from workshop slides): rank keys by a learned importance score (attention weight proxies + novelty detector). Keep top-K, compress rest with quantized PCA. Implementation note: use running EWMA of attention mass per key + a surprise score from next-token perplexity delta.

- Prefix memoization + delta encoding: store prefix outputs in a compact hashed store and replay deltas for small changes. Seems brittle but could be cheap for structured dialogs (forms, checklists). Worth sketching a small prototype for the demo app.

Random experimental ideas (to-do list):
1) Small locally reproducible benchmark: pick ~200 sample sessions from demo-prod (anonymized), instrument KV sizes and token-level importance. Measure: fraction of tokens responsible for 90% of next-token attention mass. (Hypothesis: 15% of entries carry 90% importance.)
2) Implement EWMA attention tracker in the runtime (cheap counter per KV id). Store counters as uint16 to save mem. Expose an RPC to query top-N by EWMA.
3) Micro-batching + adaptive batch width: try rules where batch size is reduced if average KV hit-rate < threshold — saves compute for low-reuse loads.
4) Prototype an "anchor encoder" off a frozen LM: small MLP on top of pooled last-layer activations to produce 64-d anchor. Store anchors in a separate fast index, train with contrastive loss to reconstruct key-space distances.

Concrete action items for next week:
- Pull 200 sessions and write the simple metric script (I can do this on Monday). Link: github issue above.
- Quick sketch of in-runtime EWMA (ask infra for safe flagging). Slack: #serving-runtime.
- Draft a brief one-pager for product about staged rollout: anchor-compression for free-tier long-sessions, strict-KV for enterprise. (Target: 1 page, 1 diagram.)

Open questions / doubts:
- How expensive is per-key EWMA maintenance at scale? We need to simulate mem overhead for pools of size 10M keys. Maybe store only for active set + sampling sketches (Count-Min?).
- Anchors: do they actually preserve causal generation quality? If anchors capture semantics but lose fine-grained pointers (dates, names), we risk hallucinations. Need fallback policy: if generation deviates from final-checkpoint tests, fallback to full KV route.

Links & references I want to re-read:
- Anchor compression (arXiv) — re-check evaluation section; look for per-domain transfer notes.
- "Eviction by surprise" slides from Ops workshop — look for pseudo-code.
- Prior internal doc: kv-shard-playbook-notes-aisha-raza-2026-06.json (for distribution constraints).

Notes-to-self (bullet chaos):
- If we do EWMA counters, think about saturating counters vs rescale epochally. 
- For demo, simpler is better: implement deterministic LRU+importance hybrid before trained anchors.
- Keep track of failure cases: multi-turn referential queries where older tokens are actually crucial. Add these to the evaluation holdout.

Short mental-models (for explaining to PMs):
- "Most of the context is dust; we only need to keep the shiny bits." -> quantify shiny bits.
- "Anchors are postcards summarizing a long beach hat of conversation." (ok, weird metaphor)

Slack reminders: ping Marco about dataset anonymization; ask Aisha about whether Count-Min is acceptable in infra layer.

Experiment sketch (pseudo):
- Sample sessions -> compute per-key attention mass with head-summed attention from a pass of 1B-token model -> rank keys -> compute cumulative mass curve -> fit 80/90/95 thresholds -> run virtual eviction sim (remove compressed keys, measure KL on next-token distribution).

Why this is different from previous attempts: we should treat compression not as a one-off lossy transform but as a routing signal: cheap anchors + fallback to exact KV for high-stakes API calls. This hybrid might buy most of the savings with acceptable risk.

End of dump. Revisit on Wed with initial metrics.
